author: A Robot
objectives: Describe Mars’s apparent retrograde path (eastward drift → westward loop → return to eastward) during an episode.
Explain why apparent retrograde motion occurs in the heliocentric model as a consequence of Earth overtaking a slower-moving outer planet.
Contrast geocentric and heliocentric explanations and articulate why heliocentrism is preferred for parsimony.
Predict when retrograde motion will occur for a given outer planet using relative orbital positions and speed.
Compare retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn and explain why more distant planets produce smaller loops.

modules.description: Students observe Mars against a star field from an Earth-based perspective, focusing on the eastward drift, slowing, westward loop, and return to eastward motion.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the three phases of Mars’s apparent retrograde episode in the sky.
Interpret direction changes in Mars’s apparent motion relative to background stars.
Practice describing an observed motion pattern before introducing physical explanations.
instructions: Keep your view pointed toward the star field.
Use Next/Previous to step through the retrograde timeline.
Track Mars’s direction: eastward drift → near-stop → westward loop → eastward resume.

clips.changeMeaning: Initial staging sets Mars at the start of the episode and shows the eastward-drift label while keeping the retrograde-loop label hidden so students focus on the observed beginning.
clips.narration: In the night sky, Mars doesn’t wander randomly. During a retrograde episode, it drifts slowly eastward against background stars—then later slows, reverses, and loops back west.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars’s marker is advanced to the right (eastward in the student view), reinforcing that its apparent position changes relative to the fixed star field.
clips.narration: As days pass, Mars creeps eastward from its earlier position among the constellations. We can track it night after night.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is positioned near the turning region where it nearly stalls; labels switch to indicate that the westward loop is about to begin.
clips.narration: Then Mars slows—its apparent eastward motion almost stops. This is where the retrograde event starts to become obvious.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is moved back to the left (westward in the student view), creating the characteristic reversal direction for the loop.
clips.narration: Next, Mars appears to move westward across the star field. That westward motion is the hallmark of retrograde looping.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars advances again to the right and the retrograde label is hidden, visually completing the full loop cycle from drift to reversal back to drift.
clips.narration: Finally, Mars resumes its eastward drift. Observing the full pattern—drift, loop, and return—was the key puzzle that motivated a new model of planetary motion.

modules.moduleName: Scene 2 — The Heliocentric Overtake Explanation (Earth vs. Mars)
modules.description: Students view a simplified outside solar-system geometry where Earth moves faster on the inner orbit and overtakes slower Mars on the outer orbit, producing the apparent retrograde loop.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Relate retrograde motion to relative orbital speeds between Earth and an outer planet.
Explain how overtaking changes the observer’s line of sight and produces an apparent direction reversal.
Use the passing-car analogy to build an intuitive geometric understanding.
instructions: Focus on Earth (inner orbit) and Mars (outer orbit).
Notice how Earth’s faster motion changes the apparent direction of Mars.
Follow the timeline until the apparent westward motion switches back to eastward.

components.text: Same idea as passing a slower car in the next lane.

clips.changeMeaning: Sets the outside-view starting geometry with Earth on the inner, faster orbit and Mars on the outer, slower orbit; both labels appear to cue the mechanism being explored.
clips.narration: From outside the solar system, the orbits are smooth. The key is relative motion: Earth’s faster inner orbit lets it overtake Mars.

clips.changeMeaning: Earth is advanced toward the longitude of Mars while Mars lags behind on the outer orbit; this sets up the changing line of sight that will correspond to slowing in the apparent motion.
clips.narration: As Earth moves ahead, the direction from Earth to Mars changes. Observers on Earth interpret that shifting line of sight as a change in Mars’s apparent motion.

clips.changeMeaning: Positions Earth and Mars closer to an alignment; this configuration corresponds to when Mars’s apparent eastward drift nearly stops before the direction reversal.
clips.narration: When Earth is nearly lined up with Mars, the apparent eastward motion of Mars slows dramatically—almost stopping.

clips.changeMeaning: After Earth passes Mars, Earth–Mars viewing geometry flips, matching the observational switch to westward motion during the retrograde loop.
clips.narration: Once Earth passes Mars, the viewing direction reverses. That is why Mars appears to move westward—creating the retrograde loop.

clips.changeMeaning: Continuing Earth’s motion carries the system beyond the turning geometry; the apparent direction for Mars returns to eastward, completing the loop explanation.
clips.narration: As Earth continues moving forward, Mars’s apparent motion returns to eastward. The loop is a natural outcome of relative orbital motion.

modules.description: Students compare a geocentric epicycle-style idea (extra constructed circles) with a heliocentric relative-motion explanation that achieves the same observational retrograde behavior with less ad hoc structure.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Describe the challenge for geocentric models: retrograde requires added epicycle machinery.
Explain why heliocentric motion generates retrograde naturally from relative orbital speeds.
Apply the concept of parsimony to choose the model with fewer arbitrary additions.
instructions: Compare the left (geocentric/epicycle) pathway vs the right (heliocentric/relative motion).
Identify which explanation requires more built-in adjustment circles.
Conclude why the heliocentric account is preferred even if both can be tuned to match data.

clips.changeMeaning: Enables both mini-diagrams side by side and aligns the markers at a shared starting configuration so students can compare complexity and structure.
clips.narration: Both models can be made to match what we see. The key question is: how much extra structure must you add to reproduce the retrograde loop?

clips.changeMeaning: The geocentric Mars marker shifts along a more intricate path, while the epicycle trail scales up to highlight additional constructed circular motion.
clips.narration: In a geocentric framework, producing the same apparent loop often requires adding epicycles—extra circles with carefully chosen sizes and speeds.

clips.changeMeaning: Earth and Mars markers move smoothly to new positions while the heliocentric trail remains simple, emphasizing that the loop arises from relative orbital motion rather than added circles.
clips.narration: In heliocentrism, Earth and Mars move on simple orbits. The apparent retrograde loop is produced by how one planet’s motion is observed from another.

clips.changeMeaning: The epicycle diagram is faded while the heliocentric relative-motion pathway stays highlighted; color accents make the parsimony conclusion visually explicit.
clips.narration: Because heliocentrism explains retrograde without introducing extra epicycles, it’s preferred on grounds of parsimony: fewer arbitrary additions, same observational outcome.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4 — Compare Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn Loop Sizes
modules.description: Students compare retrograde loops across three outer planets. The apparent loop size decreases from Mars to Jupiter to Saturn because the relative orbital-speed difference between Earth and each planet is smaller for more distant orbits.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare apparent retrograde loop magnitudes for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
Explain qualitatively why farther planets show smaller loops.
Connect loop strength to relative orbital speed differences and relative geometry.
instructions: Watch which planet’s marker moves farthest westward during retrograde.
Notice the hierarchy: Mars shows the largest loop, Saturn the smallest.
Use the final label to make a prediction for an unknown outer planet.

components.text: Farther planets → smaller relative speed difference → smaller loops.

clips.changeMeaning: All three planets start from an equivalent apparent configuration so that later westward excursions can be compared directly.
clips.narration: Retrograde loops vary by planet. Mars shows the most dramatic loop, Jupiter’s is smaller, and Saturn’s is the smallest.

clips.changeMeaning: During the retrograde interval, Mars shifts farthest westward; Jupiter and Saturn shift less, visually encoding the relative loop-size hierarchy.
clips.narration: In the retrograde phase, the apparent westward excursion is largest for Mars because Earth’s faster orbital motion differs most from Mars’s.

clips.changeMeaning: The timeline demonstrates that Jupiter’s westward excursion is intermediate while Saturn remains subtle, reinforcing that farther planets produce weaker loops.
clips.narration: Jupiter’s loop is intermediate: Earth and Jupiter’s relative orbital speeds differ less than for Mars, so the reversal is weaker.

clips.changeMeaning: Returns all planets toward their starting apparent positions to complete the comparative cycle and set up the final conceptual takeaway.
clips.narration: Saturn’s loop is the smallest. Because Saturn is farther out, Earth’s overtaking effect is diminished, producing a smaller apparent retrograde excursion.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the explanatory rule about relative speed differences and uses color accents to distinguish each planet in a final prediction-oriented check.
clips.narration: For any outer planet, predict loop strength by asking: how much faster is Earth’s orbit compared to that planet’s? Bigger speed difference means a larger loop; smaller difference means a smaller loop.
